```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
bench <- read.csv("benchmarks.csv")
machine <- read.csv("benchmarks-machine.csv")
```

Whether a GPU is worth it depends on the computation, the size of the data
and the hardware at both ends. This vignette reports what we measured, so
you can judge for your own work, including the cases where the GPU loses.

The timings below were recorded by `bench/run-benchmarks.R` in the
package's source repository, not computed when this vignette was built
(the machines that build R packages have no GPU).

## The machine

```{r machine, echo = FALSE}
knitr::kable(machine, col.names = c("", ""))
```

The CPU side is base R as most people run it: a multi-threaded BLAS on 8
cores, which is what `%*%`, `lm`, `qr` and `solve` use. `dist`, `hclust`
and `cor` do not use the BLAS and run on one core.

Each time is the median of three runs after a warm-up run, in seconds.
Data is in R's memory at the start and the result back in R's memory at the
end, so the GPU times include copying both ways.

## Results

```{r results, echo = FALSE}
tab <- bench[!is.na(bench$cpu), ]
speedup <- function(gpu) ifelse(is.na(gpu), "",
                                sprintf("%.1fx", tab$cpu / gpu))
shown <- data.frame(
  Task = tab$task, Size = tab$size,
  `base R` = sprintf("%.3f", tab$cpu),
  `GPU single` = ifelse(is.na(tab$single), "",
                        sprintf("%.3f", tab$single)),
  `speed-up` = speedup(tab$single),
  `GPU double` = sprintf("%.3f", tab$double),
  `speed-up ` = speedup(tab$double),
  check.names = FALSE)
knitr::kable(shown, align = "llrrrrr")
```

`gpuMatMult` only computes in double precision, so it has no single
column.

```{r chart, echo = FALSE, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5, fig.alt = "Speed-up of each gputools function over base R in single and double precision, on a log scale; values above 1 mean the GPU is faster."}
s <- tab$cpu / tab$single
d <- tab$cpu / tab$double
labels <- sub(" vs .*", "", tab$task)
op <- par(mar = c(4, 13, 1, 1))
barplot(t(cbind(s, d)), beside = TRUE, horiz = TRUE, log = "x",
        names.arg = labels, las = 1, xlab = "speed-up over base R (log scale)",
        legend.text = c("single", "double"),
        args.legend = list(x = "bottomright", bty = "n"))
abline(v = 1, lty = 2)
par(op)
```

## Reading the results

**Where the GPU wins.** Computations that are large, regular and many
times over the same data: Kendall's correlation (base R's is a direct
O(n^2) loop per pair of variables), Pearson's and Spearman's (one matrix
product of standardised columns on the GPU), distance matrices, Granger
tests over many pairs of series, the combined `gpuDistClust`, which keeps
the distance matrix on the GPU for the clustering, and solving and
decomposing large matrices (`gpuSolve`, `gpuPrcomp`).

**Where it does not.**

- `gpuMatMult`, `gpuLm`: a modern multi-threaded BLAS is already fast at
  these, and the GPU pays for copying the data across and back. The GPU
  here is also a workstation card with slow double precision.
- `gpuHclust` alone: the clustering is a sequence of n small dependent
  steps, which leaves the GPU mostly idle; it pays off only together with
  the distance computation (`gpuDistClust`).
- Small data of any kind: see the next section.

**Single or double precision.** Consumer and workstation GPUs run double
precision many times slower than single; data-centre GPUs do not. For
statistics whose result is a correlation, a distance or a test statistic,
single precision usually loses nothing that matters; for least squares on
badly conditioned data, use double.

## When the GPU pays off

```{r crossover-data, include = FALSE}
xo <- read.csv("crossover.csv")
xo$speedup <- xo$cpu / xo$single
xo$speedupDouble <- xo$cpu / xo$double
fns <- unique(xo$fn[!is.na(xo$cpu)])
firstAt <- function(f, k) {
  d <- xo[xo$fn == f & !is.na(xo$cpu), ]
  hit <- d$size[d$speedup >= k]
  if (length(hit)) format(min(hit), big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE) else "not reached"
}
ov <- read.csv("call-overhead.csv")
```

Every GPU call has a fixed cost: copying the data to the card and back,
starting the computation, and the first time a function is used in a
session, compiling its GPU code. On small data that fixed cost is most of
the time, and base R is faster. Each function has a size above which the
GPU wins. The table gives, for each, the smallest size tested at which it
beat base R in single precision, and at which it was at least 5 times
faster; the chart shows the whole range.

```{r crossover-table, echo = FALSE}
what <- vapply(fns, function(f) xo$what[xo$fn == f][1], "")
tested <- vapply(fns, function(f) {
  z <- range(xo$size[xo$fn == f])
  paste(format(z, big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE), collapse = " to ")
}, "")
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Function = fns, `Size measured as` = what, Tested = tested,
  `Faster than R from` = vapply(fns, firstAt, "", k = 1),
  `5 times faster from` = vapply(fns, firstAt, "", k = 5),
  check.names = FALSE, row.names = NULL))
```

```{r crossover-chart, echo = FALSE, fig.width = 7.5, fig.height = 7.5, fig.alt = "Speed-up over base R against data size for each gputools function, single and double precision, on log scales; the dashed line at 1 marks where the GPU starts to win."}
op <- par(mfrow = c(ceiling(length(fns) / 3), 3), mar = c(3.2, 3.2, 2, 0.5),
          mgp = c(2, 0.6, 0), cex = 0.7)
for (f in fns) {
  d <- xo[xo$fn == f & !is.na(xo$cpu), ]
  yr <- range(c(d$speedup, d$speedupDouble, 1), na.rm = TRUE)
  plot(d$size, d$speedup, log = "xy", type = "b", pch = 19, ylim = yr,
       xlab = d$what[1], ylab = "times faster than R", main = f)
  lines(d$size, d$speedupDouble, type = "b", pch = 1, lty = 3)
  abline(h = 1, lty = 2, col = "grey50")
}
par(op)
```

Filled points are single precision, open points double.

### Calling it well

- **Give it the whole problem in one call.** A call costs about
  `r sprintf("%.0f", 1e6 * ov$seconds[1])` µs however small the data,
  against `r sprintf("%.0f", 1e6 * ov$seconds[2])` µs for `cor()` on the
  same two columns. Correlating 1,000 pairs of columns one `gpuCor` call at
  a time took `r sprintf("%.3f", ov$seconds[3])` s, about
  `r sprintf("%.0f", ov$seconds[3] / ov$seconds[5])` times as long as the
  same loop with `cor()` (`r sprintf("%.3f", ov$seconds[5])` s). One
  `gpuCor` call on all 1,000 columns at once, computing every one of the
  million pairs, took `r sprintf("%.3f", ov$seconds[4])` s. Put the
  variables in the columns of one matrix rather than looping.
- **Below the sizes in the table, use base R.** The GPU's fixed cost is
  larger than the whole computation there.
- **The first call in a session compiles.** It adds about
  `r sprintf("%.1f", bench$single[bench$task == "kernel compile, first use of a file"])`
  s per group of functions and precision, once; time the second call when
  comparing.

## Wide data: the strongest pairs

```{r pairs-data, include = FALSE}
pp <- read.csv("pairs.csv")
fmt <- function(v) ifelse(is.na(v), "--", sprintf("%.2f", v))
```

For thousands of variables or more, the whole correlation matrix is the
problem: `r format(max(pp$variables), big.mark = ",")` variables have
`r format(max(pp$variables)^2 / 2, big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE)`
pairs, and their matrix takes
`r round(8 * max(pp$variables)^2 / 1e9)` GB. Usually only the strong
pairs are wanted. `gpuCorPairs()` returns those, every pair at or above a
threshold or each variable's strongest partners, computing the matrix on
the GPU a block at a time and never holding it whole.

The table times finding every pair with |r| >= 0.8 among variables of
`r pp$rows[1]` observations (random data with a few hundred planted
correlated groups): base R's `cor()` and then `which()`, `gpuCor()` and
then `which()`, and `gpuCorPairs()`; and, last, `gpuCorPairs()` finding
each variable's 10 strongest partners. Times are in seconds; "--" was not
run, the matrix being too big to wait for.

```{r pairs-table, echo = FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Variables = format(pp$variables, big.mark = ","),
  `Pairs found` = format(pp$pairs, big.mark = ","),
  `cor + which` = fmt(pp$cor), `gpuCor + which` = fmt(pp$gpuCor),
  gpuCorPairs = fmt(pp$gpuCorPairs), `top 10 each` = fmt(pp$top10),
  check.names = FALSE), align = "rrrrrr")
```

Most of the time `cor()` and `gpuCor()` take here goes on the matrix
itself, building it and searching it in R, which `gpuCorPairs()` never
does. Use it whenever you want pairs, not the matrix.

## Association scans

```{r assoc-data, include = FALSE}
sc <- read.csv("assoc.csv")
secs <- function(v) ifelse(is.na(v), "--", sprintf("%.2f", v))
big <- sc[!is.na(sc$MatrixEQTL), ]
big <- big[which.max(big$snps * big$genes), ]
```

`gpuAssoc()` tests every column of one matrix against every column of
another by linear regression with covariates: the scan of an eQTL study,
SNPs against genes. It computes what Matrix eQTL's linear model does
(Shabalin 2012), so the comparison is with Matrix eQTL itself, version
`r if (requireNamespace("MatrixEQTL", quietly = TRUE)) as.character(packageVersion("MatrixEQTL")) else "2.4"`,
running on the multi-threaded OpenBLAS of the machine above. Each scan
has `r sc$samples[1]` samples and `r sc$covariates[1]` covariates and
reports p <= 1e-5; both programs reported the same associations wherever
both ran.

```{r assoc-table, echo = FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  SNPs = format(sc$snps, big.mark = ","),
  Genes = format(sc$genes, big.mark = ","),
  Tests = format(sc$snps * as.double(sc$genes), big.mark = ",",
                 scientific = FALSE),
  Found = format(sc$found, big.mark = ","),
  `Matrix eQTL` = secs(sc$MatrixEQTL),
  `gpuAssoc single` = secs(sc$single), `gpuAssoc double` = secs(sc$double),
  check.names = FALSE), align = "rrrrrrr")
```

Times are in seconds; "--" was not run (at four billion tests Matrix eQTL
ran out of a 48 GB job's memory). At
`r format(big$snps * as.double(big$genes), big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE)`
tests the GPU was `r round(big$MatrixEQTL / big$single)` times as fast.
A genome-wide scan, millions of SNPs, is a loop over chromosomes or
blocks of SNPs, each call large enough to keep the GPU busy.

## Your own hardware

To measure your own machine, run from a checkout of the source repository
with gputools installed:

```sh
Rscript bench/run-benchmarks.R my-results
```
